A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the global-scale representation of North America has a regionalized structure, and that the representation of the global-scale distances is consistent with a power law, although the power law is an artifact of the regionalized structure of the representation and not a property of the representation per se.
we have found that the global-scale representation of North American geography is a complex, but not necessarily inconsistent, amalgamation of psychological regions and beliefs.

global-scale judgments are not generated from common representations but are instead generated from a variety of representations and strategies, including those that are relative, absolute, and regionalized.

the global-scale representations of latitude and distance that underlie our judgments are not the same as the physical distances and locations that are measured by geographers.

the global-scale representations of latitude and distance that underlie judgments are not only regionalized, but also that the regionalization is psychologically real, in that people's judgments of the locations and distances between places reflect the same regional structure that they perceive.
